newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Socialist says will stick to euro timetable.
newsitem.headline: French Socialist says will stick to euro timetable.

text.p: France's new Socialist-led government plans to stick to the timetable for launching a single European currency in 1999, a senior Socialist said on Tuesday.
"Of course we must respect this deadline," Elisabeth Guigou, tipped to serve as European Affairs Minister in the new government, told RTL radio.

The Socialists however made no declarations which shed light on how they planned to shift the direction Europe was taking as it prepared for a single currency without derailing economic and monetary union.
The party, swept to power by a parliamentary election victory on Sunday, has said it wants assurances that Europe no longer means austerity.

Most controversially, it has said it wants to renegotiate the European Union "stability pact" meant to limit budget deficits after the launch of the euro and agreed in Dublin last year after lengthy negotiations.
New French Prime Minister Lionel Jospin said during the election campaign he did not feel bound to it.

"The stability pact adds conditions which do not feature in the Maastricht treaty. The pact is a 'super Maastricht' of sorts and a concession which the French government made absurdly to the Germans or certain German circles," Jospin said on May 20.
"Therefore I have no reason to feel committed to it," he said in an interview with Le Monde which appeared just before the Socialists' surprise win in a first round of voting.
Any attempt to renegotiate the stability pact, seen by Germany as a key guarantee of fiscal discipline after the launch of the euro, could create serious problems on the way to EMU.
Financial markets have been waiting to see how many of the Socialists' pledges made during the campaign are translated into actual policy after the new government is named this week.
In the meantime they have given Jospin the benefit of the doubt, marking up the franc, bonds and stocks after an initial steep drop.
But analysts say even if Jospin did want to back off from his resistance to the stability pact, he would have a hard time with domestic opinion if he were to sign up to it too quickly.
The pact was due to be signed at a European Union summit in Amsterdam this month, where Jospin is expected to accompany President Jacques Chirac.
"If they are serious about renegotiation they have to postpone the ratification of the pact," AMN Amro economist Philippe Brossard said.

Or if Jospin allowed it through, "he starts going against his promises, there will be a row between the Socialists and their (parliamentary) allies and disenchantment in the country", he said. "The situtation is rather blocked. It depends on the strength of their opinion and how much gambling they want to do," he said.
Jospin has avoided any substantial policy statements since the left's victory on Sunday. Other senior Socialists were unavailable for comment.
